I actually am exploring exactly this. Ironically from the perspective of someone that was trying to leave the Terminal.

How i got here i find kinda interesting. Originally i was trying to leave the terminal. Using GPUI/etc frameworks. I kept running into the terminal though, because no matter how nice the UI is - the terminal still needs to work excellently.

Eventually i decided to try an abomination. To use a custom terminal which, not unlike Kitty images, allows generic apps to pass escape codes to control the UI components. Where the UI components have no restriction on "dumb terminals". So my text editor is a two part app, an editor and a tty to render the actual custom UI APC codes.

This paved the way for true smooth scrolling from within a terminal editor, as the editor effectively paginates but the tty scrolls within the buffered pages. It allows for different UI components to mix fonts and font sizes, eg popup docs being a different size than the other text, and .. well, anything i suppose.

I have to say it's working excellently and is slowly becoming my daily driver. I won't link it though, it's a fully vibe coded and even claude designed horror.

I'm surprised i've not seen more of this in the past to be honest.

joshka · Nov 14, 2026

Yep,and I want to do that too :)

I've written about it before, but in brief the mountain of standards is worth ripping out wholesale and doing write as a semantic protocol. It's needed to solve several things that work really poorly in terminals because their unit of compatibility is cells rather than a higher primitive. It's hard to bake something on top that works well.

The need is most strong in Accessibility, Text wrapping, Scrollback handling (i.e. making the scrollback editable and not dead text), and various other bits that make writing highly functional TUIs. Coding agents tend to find all those edge cases.

This often gets push back that it's easy, to which I can point nay sayers at the various many months long issues on things in Codex, Gemini, Claude etc. on flickering, scrolling, key handline, IME, ... doing anything moderately complex involves modeling a terminal in a terminal app effectively.

Ghostty and Rex sort of do the opposite bit. If you think of it like a stack, they write a new layer underneath that transports the cells on a better multiplexer layer 0. I think a new semantic layer 2 is an approach that would be neat to work with.

A pet peeve of mine is that most people / WM get "useless gaps" wrong. You do want a gap between two terminals because otherwise there are times where things can get really confusing (where you don't know what belong to which terminal / window).

So the "borderless" (0 pixels) / zero "useless gaps" simply are confusing and... Wrong.

But then people who do use useless gap, as in TFA, get it wrong too: they typically add gaps near the monitor's edges.

Yeah. But no. Sorry but my monitor's edge is a perfectly fine gap. I don't risk mistaking it for anything.

So I modified my WM (the Awesome WM) to do proper "useless gaps" computation and remove the ones that really are useless: and that'd be those near the monitor's physical border.

I mean: nearly everybody gets it wrong, but it's not complicated to get it right, is it?

P.S: even the terminology is wrong... People calling those "useless gaps" haven't got a clue: they are useful. The only useless ones are the one on the monitor's edge (if your monitor has physical edges, which it probably does).

favori995749721 · Nov 14, 2026

One benefit worth calling out: the box-drawing fallback is worse than it looks for CJK users. U+2500-257F and the half/full block elements are East Asian "Ambiguous" in UAX #11, so in a terminal configured to render ambiguous as double width (xterm's cjkWidth, iTerm2's checkbox) every line glyph takes two cells and the whole frame lands in the wrong place. Cell borders aren't text, so that failure class just disappears.

The part I'd want specced early: borders are per-cell, but cells aren't per-grapheme. A CJK char owns two cells plus a continuation placeholder, and combining marks or ZWJ emoji sequences own zero-or-more depending on whose wcwidth table you ask, so app and terminal routinely disagree across Unicode versions. Today that shows up as a vertical bar one column off; with cell borders it becomes a line that stops short of the corner. Does the border attach to the cell or to the grapheme cluster?
